newsitem.title: CHINA: China names diplomat to head Xinhua in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: China names diplomat to head Xinhua in Hong Kong.

text.p: China announced on Friday the appointment of diplomat Jiang Enzhu to head the Hong Kong branch of its Xinhua news agency, which until the July 1 handover of sovereignty acted as Beijing's main voice in the territory.
Jiang, 59, Chinese ambassador to Britain until early this year, was appointed recently to his new post by the State Council, or cabinet, the Xinhua news agency said.
Both Xinhua and the State Council declined to give details of the appointment or to comment on Jiang's role in Hong Kong following the July 1 end of British rule in the territory.
Before the return of Hong Kong to Chinese sovereignty, the Xinhua chief in the territory was a key agent of Beijing's policies towards its British colonial administration.

The Xinhua mission acted somewhat like a shadow government in Hong Kong, with deputy directors tracking specific policy areas -- a role that is likely to be greatly reduced now Hong Kong is ruled by a China-backed post-colonial administration.

The Hong Kong Apple Daily newspaper, which earlier this month predicted Jiang Enzhu's appointment to replace Zhou Nan, 70, as Xinhua head, said the agency's staffing and organisation in the region would soon undergo major changes.

"Nearly one-third of its departmental and bureau-level departments will be abolished and all of its six incumbent deputy directors also plan to leave their posts one after another by the end of the year," the newspaper said.

However, analysts said the agency was expected to continue to act as a political liaison post for Beijing in the new special administrative region, as well as carrying out its core function as a news agency.

Hong Kong newspapers had earlier speculated that Jiang, a former vice foreign minister, would become head of the new Foreign Ministry's office in Hong Kong, but that job went to his predecessor in London, Ma Yuzhen.

The post-handover Foreign Ministry office will handle Hong Kong's external affairs -- one of the few areas of its government controlled directly from Beijing's -- and will serve as a communications channel to the central government.

China has been at pains to stress that it will not interfere in Hong Kong's capitalist system or local administration for 50 years, as promised under the terms of the Sino-British agreement that ended 156 years of colonial rule from London.
Beijing this month disbanded its hand-picked Hong Kong Preparatory Committee, which had paved the way for the creation of China's post-colonial government in the region.
